idiom_name: private static fields + public instance properties
implementation_notes: In C# the classic form is literal: private static fields hold the state and public instance properties read and write them, so new LogSettings() creates an ordinary object whose data is shared with every sibling. The runtime loads and initializes the type's statics before the type is first referenced, and they live for the application domain's lifetime - exactly the pattern's well-defined lifetime. Nothing here replaces the classic structure: static fields are the mechanism and the instance side is the interface; keep this form when a container, XAML loader or serializer must construct the type while the data is application-wide.
pitfalls: Static fields live for the application domain: unit tests inherit each other's writes and there is no per-test instance to construct, so a reset seam (or an instance-based state holder) is mandatory for testable code.

Writes to non-volatile static fields are unsynchronized: use lock/Interlocked/volatile for single fields and a lock for compound updates, because two instances writing concurrently race even though each call looks local.
A constructor that writes shared state makes construction order observable process-wide, and derived types share the same static fields, so a subclass silently overwrites the base monostate's data.

variants.name: C# 8 interface with protected static fields and default property implementations
variants.idiom_name: interface with protected static state and default property implementations
variants.implementation_notes: C# 8 default interface implementations let the interface itself own the static storage and the property behaviour, so a class gets the monostate by implementing an otherwise empty interface and can still override individual members for variants (a manager that adds an offset) while sharing the interface's static fields. Prefer this variant when several related types must share one storage but the shared members should be declared once instead of being repeated per class; the classic per-class form remains right when each type needs its own storage.
pitfalls: Static interface members exist once per interface type, so every implementer shares the same storage and there is no per-class copy unless the class declares its own members.
With explicit interface implementation the members are invisible on the class type, so callers must hold the interface type; that is the intended seam but it surprises consumers.
Default interface members require C# 8 and a runtime that supports them - older Unity profiles and targets will not compile or run the default bodies.
